style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ctx-t.name: p03-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $\min\frac12\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$; constraint $y_i(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i+b)\ge1$; convex quadratic program.

p03-fig-title.name: p03-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fig-title.text: From maximizing distance to minimizing the norm

p03-c2-t.name: p03-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-c2-t.text:
The objective is convex quadratic and the constraints are linear, so a local minimum is global
Going deeper: put a multiplier $\alpha_i$ on each constraint to get the Lagrangian $L=\frac12\|\mathbf{w}\|^2+\sum_i\alpha_i[1-y_i(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i+b)]$
Maximum distance equals minimum norm: a small norm makes $\gamma=1/\|\mathbf{w}\|$ large

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-fig-title.name: p04-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-c2-t.name: p04-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-c2-t.text:
Dual: maximize $\sum\alpha_i-\frac12\sum\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf{x}_i^T\mathbf{x}_j$, with $\alpha_i\ge0$, $\sum\alpha_iy_i=0$
If $\alpha_i>0$, that point must lie on a support plane; the converse may fail, since degenerate data can have boundary points with a multiplier of 0 in some optimal solution
The inner-product form leaves a door open to kernel methods, but computing inner products still depends on feature dimension; cost is not independent of dimension

p04-ban-t.text: Takeaway: points with positive multipliers lie on the boundary, and only they take part in prediction.

p09-c2-t.name: p09-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p09-c2-t.text:
First find where the classes are closest: the largest negative $-1$, the smallest positive $3$; the boundary is the midpoint $(3+(-1))/2=1$
Half width $=(3-(-1))/2=2$, full width $=4$; matching $w=0.5$, $b=-0.5$, so $3$ and $-1$ score exactly $\pm1$
Points 4, 5 and -2 score beyond $\pm 1$, not on the boundary, multiplier 0

steps.label: Goal: among separating… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: among separating… · 1/3 · Female: Last unit chose a linear boundary by probability. This unit turns to geometry: several lines separate the data, so which leaves the biggest buffer? Picture drawing a road between houses on both sides.

narration.label: s1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Last unit chose a linear boundary by probability. This unit turns to geometry: several lines separate the data, so which leaves the biggest buffer? Picture drawing a road between houses on both sides.

steps.label: Goal: among separating… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: among separating… · 2/3 · Male: Three goals: tell scores, geometric distance, half width and full width apart; derive the primal and dual problems from the constraints; and use the square example to show the boundary is unique while the multipliers may not be.

narration.label: s2.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Three goals: tell scores, geometric distance, half width and full width apart; derive the primal and dual problems from the constraints; and use the square example to show the boundary is unique while the multipliers may not be.

steps.label: Goal: among separating… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: among separating… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: when many lines separate the data, pick the one leaving the largest buffer. The analogy only explains space; it does not guarantee new data are all right.

narration.label: s3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: when many lines separate the data, pick the one leaving the largest buffer. The analogy only explains space; it does not guarantee new data are all right.

steps.label: Scores can be scaled; only… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Scores can be scaled; only… · 1/3 · Male: Look at one line, coefficients 1 and 0, score 1. Multiply all coefficients by 2: the line has not moved, yet the score becomes 2. Think: did the safe distance change?

narration.label: s4.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Look at one line, coefficients 1 and 0, score 1. Multiply all coefficients by 2: the line has not moved, yet the score becomes 2. Think: did the safe distance change?

steps.label: Scores can be scaled; only… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Scores can be scaled; only… · 2/3 · Female: No. The score must be divided by the normal vector's length to be a real distance. So the half width gamma is 1 over the length of w, and the full width W between the two support planes is 2 over the length of w.

narration.label: s5.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: No. The score must be divided by the normal vector's length to be a real distance. So the half width gamma is 1 over the length of w, and the full width W between the two support planes is 2 over the length of w.

steps.label: Scores can be scaled; only… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Scores can be scaled; only… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: to compare safe distance, look at gamma after dividing by the length, not the raw score. The source says margin 1 and the professor's notes say full width 2; those are half width and full width, two ways of saying it.

narration.label: s6.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: to compare safe distance, look at gamma after dividing by the length, not the raw score. The source says margin 1 and the professor's notes say full width 2; those are half width and full width, two ways of saying it.

steps.label: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 1/3 · Female: With distance defined, we now pick, among all feasible boundaries, the shortest normal vector. Maximizing distance is equivalent to minimizing half the squared length of w, with every point's score at least 1.

narration.label: s7.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: With distance defined, we now pick, among all feasible boundaries, the shortest normal vector. Maximizing distance is equivalent to minimizing half the squared length of w, with every point's score at least 1.

steps.label: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 2/3 · Male: This is a convex quadratic objective with linear constraints, so a local minimum is global. But convexity alone does not guarantee every variable is unique; it takes the weights' strict convexity plus two separable classes to establish the optimal boundary.

narration.label: s8.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: This is a convex quadratic objective with linear constraints, so a local minimum is global. But convexity alone does not guarantee every variable is unique; it takes the weights' strict convexity plus two separable classes to establish the optimal boundary.

steps.label: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Primal: maximizing distance is… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: among all separating lines, pick the one with the shortest normal vector. Going deeper, put a multiplier on each constraint and we get the Lagrangian.

narration.label: s9.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: among all separating lines, pick the one with the shortest normal vector. Going deeper, put a multiplier on each constraint and we get the Lagrangian.

steps.label: Dual: weights are a… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Dual: weights are a… · 1/3 · Male: Set the Lagrangian's partial derivatives with respect to the weights and the intercept to zero. The weights equal the sum of multiplier times label times feature, and the sum of multiplier times label is zero. Substitute back, and only the multipliers remain.

narration.label: s10.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Set the Lagrangian's partial derivatives with respect to the weights and the intercept to zero. The weights equal the sum of multiplier times label times feature, and the sum of multiplier times label is zero. Substitute back, and only the multipliers remain.

steps.label: Dual: weights are a… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Dual: weights are a… · 2/3 · Female: Complementary slackness says: multiplier times margin minus 1 is zero. So a point with a positive multiplier must lie on a support plane; the converse may fail, since degenerate data can have a boundary point with multiplier zero. Think: what about points far from the boundary?

narration.label: s11.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Complementary slackness says: multiplier times margin minus 1 is zero. So a point with a positive multiplier must lie on a support plane; the converse may fail, since degenerate data can have a boundary point with multiplier zero. Think: what about points far from the boundary?

steps.label: Dual: weights are a… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Dual: weights are a… · 3/3 · Male: Their multiplier is zero, and they do not take part in prediction. Take this away: points with positive multipliers lie on the boundary, and only they take part in prediction. The inner-product form opens a door to kernel methods, but computing inner products still depends on feature dimension.

narration.label: s12.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Their multiplier is zero, and they do not take part in prediction. Take this away: points with positive multipliers lie on the boundary, and only they take part in prediction. The inner-product form opens a door to kernel methods, but computing inner products still depends on feature dimension.

steps.label: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 1/3 · Female: Now the square. The positives are 1, 1 and 1, minus 1; the negatives are minus 1, 1 and minus 1, minus 1. Take w equal 1, 0 and b equal 0, so the score is the first coordinate. Predict: what are the four labeled scores?

narration.label: s13.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Now the square. The positives are 1, 1 and 1, minus 1; the negatives are minus 1, 1 and minus 1, minus 1. Take w equal 1, 0 and b equal 0, so the score is the first coordinate. Predict: what are the four labeled scores?

steps.label: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 2/3 · Male: All 1. All four points are on the support lines. The length of w is 1, so the half width gamma is 1, and the full width W between the two support lines is 2.

narration.label: s14.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: All 1. All four points are on the support lines. The length of w is 1, so the half width gamma is 1, and the full width W between the two support lines is 2.

steps.label: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Square :w=(1,0): four scores  1… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: in this example the half width is 1 and the full width is 2, with all four points on the boundary. The source says margin 1 and the professor's notes say full width 2; that is only a convention for half versus full width.

narration.label: s15.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: in this example the half width is 1 and the full width is 2, with all four points on the boundary. The source says margin 1 and the professor's notes say full width 2; that is only a convention for half versus full width.

steps.label: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 1/3 · Male: Switch to another line, w equal 2, 1, which also separates the four points. The scores are 3, 1, minus 1, minus 3, the smallest times the label is 1, so it is still feasible. Predict: is its full width larger or smaller than 2?

narration.label: s16.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Switch to another line, w equal 2, 1, which also separates the four points. The scores are 3, 1, minus 1, minus 3, the smallest times the label is 1, so it is still feasible. Predict: is its full width larger or smaller than 2?

steps.label: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 2/3 · Female: Smaller. The full width is 2 over root 5, about 0.894, less than half of the optimal boundary's 2. Both figures use the same four points and equal-scale axes, so we can compare them directly.

narration.label: s17.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Smaller. The full width is 2 over root 5, about 0.894, less than half of the optimal boundary's 2. Both figures use the same four points and equal-scale axes, so we can compare them directly.

steps.label: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Tilted boundary :w=(2,1) also… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: many lines separate, but full width 0.894 cannot match full width 2. That is why we maximize the margin.

narration.label: s18.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: many lines separate, but full width 0.894 cannot match full width 2. That is why we maximize the margin.

steps.label: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 1/3 · Female: The boundary is unique, but what about the multipliers? In this point order, take the multipliers as t, one half minus t, t, one half minus t. For any t between 0 and one half, the weights are 1, 0. Think: is there only one set of multipliers?

narration.label: s19.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The boundary is unique, but what about the multipliers? In this point order, take the multipliers as t, one half minus t, t, one half minus t. For any t between 0 and one half, the weights are 1, 0. Think: is there only one set of multipliers?

steps.label: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 2/3 · Male: No. At t equal 0.25 all four multipliers are 0.25; at t equal 0 only points 2 and 4 are 0.5, yet all four points are still on the boundary. The dual objective is one half in every case.

narration.label: s20.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: No. At t equal 0.25 all four multipliers are 0.25; at t equal 0 only points 2 and 4 are 0.5, yet all four points are still on the boundary. The dual objective is one half in every case.

steps.label: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Non-unique multipliers: one w has… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the boundary is unique, but the multipliers form a whole family. Part of the source's multiplier equations disagree with the point order, so we recompute from the definition.

narration.label: s21.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the boundary is unique, but the multipliers form a whole family. Part of the source's multiplier equations disagree with the point order, so we recompute from the definition.

steps.label: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 1/3 · Male: A common myth: a nonsupport point can move anywhere without changing the model. Think: if we move it inside the margin, does that still hold?

narration.label: s22.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: A common myth: a nonsupport point can move anywhere without changing the model. Think: if we move it inside the margin, does that still hold?

steps.label: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 2/3 · Female: No. Only if the moved point still meets the old optimal boundary's constraints do the old solution stay feasible and optimal; move it inside the margin or to the other side and the problem changes. In practice, use tolerances to check feasibility, dual balance and primal-dual gap.

narration.label: s23.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: No. Only if the moved point still meets the old optimal boundary's constraints do the old solution stay feasible and optimal; move it inside the margin or to the other side and the problem changes. In practice, use tolerances to check feasibility, dual balance and primal-dual gap.

steps.label: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: nonsupport points can move… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: whether a nonsupport point can move depends on whether the constraints still hold afterward. If the classes are not separable at all, the hard constraints have no feasible solution, and the next unit uses slack variables.

narration.label: s24.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: whether a nonsupport point can move depends on whether the constraints still hold afterward. If the classes are not separable at all, the hard constraints have no feasible solution, and the next unit uses slack variables.

steps.label: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 1/3 · Female: Your turn. One-dimensional data: positives 3, 4, 5, negatives minus 1, minus 2. Find the boundary, the full width, and the boundary points. Hint: first find where the two classes are closest.

narration.label: s25.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Your turn. One-dimensional data: positives 3, 4, 5, negatives minus 1, minus 2. Find the boundary, the full width, and the boundary points. Hint: first find where the two classes are closest.

steps.label: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 2/3 · Male: The closest are minus 1 and 3. The boundary is their midpoint, equal to 1; the half width is 2 and the full width is 4; correspondingly w equals 0.5 and b equals minus 0.5, so 3 and minus 1 score exactly plus and minus 1. Points 4, 5 and minus 2 are not on the boundary.

narration.label: s26.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: The closest are minus 1 and 3. The boundary is their midpoint, equal to 1; the half width is 2 and the full width is 4; correspondingly w equals 0.5 and b equals minus 0.5, so 3 and minus 1 score exactly plus and minus 1. Points 4, 5 and minus 2 are not on the boundary.

steps.label: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Practice: 1D positives 3, 4, 5… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the boundary is x equal 1, the full width is 4, and only 3 and minus 1 are on the boundary. Next question: when the data cannot all be right, which condition should we relax? The next unit covers the soft margin.

narration.label: s27.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the boundary is x equal 1, the full width is 4, and only 3 and minus 1 are on the boundary. Next question: when the data cannot all be right, which condition should we relax? The next unit covers the soft margin.
